claim: Escherichia coli TF consists of 432 amino acids, comprising RBD (residues 1 to 112), PPD (residues 150 to 246), and SBD (residues 113 to 149 and 247 to 432).
source: Escherichia coli TF consists of 432 amino acids, comprising RBD (residues 1 to 112), PPD (residues 150 to 246), and SBD (residues 113 to 149 and 247 to 432) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1A showing the structure with labeled domains.

claim: MALS and analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) experiments yielded a dimerization dissociation constant (Kd) of ~ 2 μM.
source: MALS and analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) experiments yielded a dimerization dissociation constant (Kd) of ~ 2 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D), which is similar to previously reported values (Kaiser et al., 2006; Maier et al., 2003; Morgado et al., 2017).
evidence: The Kd value is determined from experimental MALS and AUC data shown in the referenced figures and is consistent with cited literature.

claim: TF monomerization induced by substrate binding was previously reported and has been further corroborated in the present work by MALS and NMR.
source: TF monomerization induced by substrate binding was previously reported (Saio et al., 2014) and has been further corroborated in the present work by MALS and NMR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by both previous literature citation and new experimental data from MALS and NMR.

claim: The intrinsic dissociation rate (kdiss) of the TF dimer is ~10 s−1.
source: Fitting of the data to a single exponential function resulted in kdiss of ~10 s−1, which indicates that the dimer is quite dynamic and thus the exchange between formation and dissociation of the dimer can be a major cause of the line broadening observed for the resonances located in RBD (Morgado et al., 2017) (Saio et al., 2014).
evidence: The kdiss value is determined from experimental data fitted to a single exponential function.

claim: The dimer is quite dynamic with a residence time of ~ 100 ms.
source: The dissociation rate (kdiss) of the dimer is ~ 10 s−1 indicating a rather dynamic TF dimer with a residence time of ~ 100 ms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The residence time is calculated from the measured dissociation rate.

claim: TF forms a symmetric dimer in a head-to-tail orientation.
source: TF forms a symmetric dimer in a head-to-tail orientation.
evidence: This is a direct structural observation from the NMR-determined structure.

claim: Part of RBD inserts into a large cavity that is formed between the SBD and PPD of the other subunit.
source: Part of RBD inserts into a large cavity that is formed between the SBD and PPD of the other subunit (Figure 2A and B) and the arrangement results in three major interfaces that hold the dimer together (Figure 2C).
evidence: This structural feature is directly observed in the NMR structure shown in the figures.

claim: A total surface of 6,670 Å2 is buried upon dimer formation.
source: A total surface of 6,670 Å2 is buried upon dimer formation.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the structural data.

claim: A triple amino-acid substitution variant (V39E/I76E/I80A; hereafter TFmon) abolishes TF dimerization.
source: The extensive interface seen in the structure to mediate the dimer was tested by mutagenesis and a triple amino-acid substitution variant (V39E/I76E/I80A; hereafter TFmon) was identified that abolishes TF dimerization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments with results shown in the referenced figure.

claim: With respect to SBD, RBD undergoes a 60° rotation and a 21 Å translation when transitioning from monomeric to dimeric state.
source: With respect to SBD, RBD undergoes a 60° rotation and a 21 Å translation, whereas PPD undergoes a 74° rotation and a 19 Å translation.
evidence: These values are calculated from structural comparison between monomeric and dimeric TF structures.

claim: PPD undergoes a 74° rotation and a 19 Å translation when transitioning from monomeric to dimeric state.
source: With respect to SBD, RBD undergoes a 60° rotation and a 21 Å translation, whereas PPD undergoes a 74° rotation and a 19 Å translation.
evidence: These values are calculated from structural comparison between monomeric and dimeric TF structures.

claim: These conformational changes result in a more compact TF structure in the dimeric form, which is consistent with small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data.
source: These conformational changes results in a more compact TF structure in the dimeric form, which is consistent with small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) data (Ries et al., 2017).
evidence: The structural observation is corroborated by independent SAXS data from cited literature.

claim: TF uses five distinct binding sites to interact with unfolded substrates such as the maltose binding protein (MBP).
source: TF uses five distinct binding sites (Figure 3B) to interact with unfolded substrates such as the maltose binding protein (MBP) (Saio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on previous structural work cited and shown in the figure.

claim: Four of the substrate-binding sites are located in SBD (A-D) and the fifth one (E) is located in PPD.
source: Four of these substrate-binding sites are located in SBD (A-D) and the fifth one (E) is located in PPD.
evidence: This is a direct description of the structural features shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the dimeric form of TF only two (A and D) among the five substrate-binding sites are fully accessible for binding, whereas the other three (B, C, and E) are partially occluded.
source: In the dimeric form of TF only two (A and D) among these five substrate-binding sites are fully accessible for binding, whereas the other three (B, C, and E) are partially occluded (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a structural observation from the dimeric TF structure shown in the figure.

claim: A protein substrate typically engages at least four of the binding sites.
source: A protein substrate typically engages at least four of the binding sites (Saio et al., 2014); thus, complex formation between TF and an unfolded protein requires that TF monomerize, as supported by NMR and MALS data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,E and F) (Saio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on previous structural work and supported by experimental data.

claim: Complex formation between TF and an unfolded protein requires that TF monomerize.
source: A protein substrate typically engages at least four of the binding sites (Saio et al., 2014); thus, complex formation between TF and an unfolded protein requires that TF monomerize, as supported by NMR and MALS data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,E and F) (Saio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a logical inference from the structural data showing that multiple binding sites are occluded in the dimer, supported by experimental evidence.

claim: The concentration of TF in the cell is ~50 μM.
source: The concentration of TF in the cell (~50 μM) is 2 to 3-fold that of the ribosome (Patzelt et al., 2002), and given the low Kd of dimerization (~2 μM) the vast majority of free TF in the cytoplasm will exist in the dimeric form.
evidence: This is based on cited literature providing cellular concentration measurements.

claim: The concentration of TF in the cell is 2 to 3-fold that of the ribosome.
source: The concentration of TF in the cell (~50 μM) is 2 to 3-fold that of the ribosome (Patzelt et al., 2002), and given the low Kd of dimerization (~2 μM) the vast majority of free TF in the cytoplasm will exist in the dimeric form.
evidence: This is based on cited literature comparing TF and ribosome concentrations.

claim: Given the low Kd of dimerization (~2 μM) the vast majority of free TF in the cytoplasm will exist in the dimeric form.
source: The concentration of TF in the cell (~50 μM) is 2 to 3-fold that of the ribosome (Patzelt et al., 2002), and given the low Kd of dimerization (~2 μM) the vast majority of free TF in the cytoplasm will exist in the dimeric form.
evidence: This is an inference based on the measured Kd and cellular concentration.

claim: Dimeric TF was substantially more efficient at suppressing aggregation than the monomeric TF.
source: The results showed that dimeric TF was substantially more efficient at suppressing aggregation than the monomeric TF (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aggregation assay data shown in the figures.

claim: In the case of shorter substrate OmpA1-192, the difference in the anti-aggregation activity between the dimeric TF and monomeric TF is much less pronounced and both species are equally efficient in suppressing aggregation.
source: The results showed that in the case of shorter substrate, which has a smaller number of hydrophobic regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), the difference in the anti-aggregation activity between the dimeric TF and monomeric TF is much less pronounced and both species are equally efficient in suppressing aggregation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by aggregation assay data comparing GAPDH and OmpA substrates.

claim: At 1:1 stoichiometric ratio with MBP, TFmon had a minimal effect on MBP folding whereas dimeric TF had a pronounced effect.
source: At 1:1 stoichiometric ratio with MBP, TFmon had a minimal effect on MBP folding whereas dimeric TF had a pronounced effect (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MBP refolding assay data shown in the figure.

claim: Dimeric TF increased the apparent folding rate of MBP and at the same time increased the yield of the soluble fraction substantially.
source: Specifically, dimeric TF increased the apparent folding rate of MBP and at the same time increased the yield of the soluble fraction substantially (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by MBP refolding assay data shown in the figures.

claim: The increase in the apparent folding rate is likely due to the most efficient suppression of aggregation by the dimeric TF.
source: The increase in the apparent folding rate is likely due to the most efficient suppression of aggregation by the dimeric TF (Apetri and Horwich, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and cited literature on chaperone mechanisms.

claim: A much higher TFmon concentration was needed to match the chaperone activity of the dimeric TF.
source: Notably, a much higher TFmon concentration was needed to match the chaperone activity of the dimeric TF (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-dependent refolding assay data.

claim: The dimeric TF was observed to have a strong 'holdase' effect on the mutant MBP as evidenced by the suppression of the folding of MBPY283D.
source: The dimeric TF was observed to have a strong 'holdase' effect on the mutant MBP as evidenced by the suppression of the folding of MBPY283D (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by refolding assay data for the MBPY283D mutant.

claim: TFmon slightly accelerated folding of MBPY283D.
source: In contrast, TFmon slightly accelerated folding (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by refolding assay data for the MBPY283D mutant.

claim: All assays showed that the monomeric and dimeric TF states have distinct chaperone activities.
source: Taken together, all assays showed that the monomeric and dimeric TF states have distinct chaperone activities.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental assays presented.

claim: ITC showed that TFmon has a 5-fold higher affinity (Kd ~ 6 μM) for protein substrates than the dimeric TF (Kd ~ 35 μM).
source: ITC showed that TFmon has a 5-fold higher affinity (Kd ~ 6 μM) for protein substrates than the dimeric TF (Kd ~ 35 μM) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is measured directly by ITC experiments shown in the figure.

claim: Unfolded PhoA binds TFmon with a kon ~ 0.5 × 106 M−1 s−1 and dissociates with a koff ~ 6 s−1.
source: Specifically, unfolded PhoA binds TFmon with a kon ~ 0.5 × 106 M−1 s−1 and dissociates with a koff ~ 6 s−1.
evidence: These kinetic parameters are measured by stopped-flow fluorescence spectroscopy.

claim: Dimeric TF binds PhoA with a 2-fold faster association rate (kon ~ 1.1 × 106 M−1 s−1) and dissociates with a 5-fold faster dissociation rate (koff ~ 30 s−1).
source: In comparison, dimeric TF binds PhoA with a 2-fold faster association rate (kon ~ 1.1 × 106 M−1 s−1) and dissociates with a 5-fold faster dissociation rate (koff ~ 30 s−1).
evidence: These kinetic parameters are measured by stopped-flow fluorescence spectroscopy.

claim: The faster association of non-native proteins with the dimeric TF over the monomeric TF is consistent with the stronger holdase activity of dimeric TF.
source: The faster association of non-native proteins with the dimeric TF over the monomeric TF is consistent with the stronger holdase activity of dimeric TF (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the kinetic data with the functional assay results.

claim: The holdase activity of a chaperone is determined by the difference between the folding rate of the substrate protein and the association rate between the chaperone and the unfolded substrate protein, as shown by kinetic experiments on SecB and TF.
source: Note that the holdase activity of a chaperone is determined by the difference between the folding rate of the substrate protein and the association rate between the chaperone and the unfolded substrate protein, as shown by kinetic experiments on SecB and TF (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited literature describing chaperone kinetics.

claim: The association rate of dimeric TF for the substrate appears to be fast enough to delay the folding of the slowly folding mutant MBPY283D, but not fast enough to delay the folding of wild type MBP.
source: Thus the association rate of dimeric TF for the substrate appears to be fast enough to delay the folding of the slowly folding mutant MBPY283D, but not fast enough to delay the folding of wild type MBP (Figure 4C and E).
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data and the observed effects on different substrates.

claim: Assembly of the dimer brings next to each other substrate-binding sites A, B, and D in the two subunits.
source: Although three out of the five substrate-binding sites are partially occluded in the dimeric TF, assembly of the dimer brings next to each other substrate-binding sites A, B, and D in the two subunits.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the dimeric TF structure.

claim: The substrate-binding sites are located within a large cavity that is accessible to unfolded proteins and present to the substrate a large contiguous binding surface that may account for the enhanced association rates of substrates with the dimeric TF.
source: The sites are located within a large cavity that is accessible to unfolded proteins (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and present to the substrate a large contiguous binding surface that may account for the enhanced association rates of substrates with the dimeric TF.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural observations that explains the kinetic data.

claim: TF is the only ribosome-associated chaperone in bacteria.
source: The trigger factor (TF) chaperone has several unique features (Hoffmann et al., 2010; Ries et al., 2017; Wruck et al., 2018): (i) is the only ribosome-associated chaperone in bacteria;
evidence: This is stated as a known feature of TF with supporting citations.

claim: With an estimated cellular concentration of ~50 μM TF is the most abundant chaperone.
source: (ii) with an estimated cellular concentration of ~50 μM (Crooke et al., 1988) it is also the most abundant one;
evidence: This is stated with a citation providing the concentration measurement.

claim: In contrast to other oligomeric chaperones such as GroEL, SecB, and Hsp90 that form stable oligomers, TF undergoes a dynamic transition between a monomeric and a dimeric form.
source: (iii) in contrast to other oligomeric chaperones such as GroEL, SecB, and Hsp90 that form stable oligomers, TF undergoes a dynamic transition between a monomeric and a dimeric form;
evidence: This is a comparative statement based on known properties of different chaperones.

claim: TF functions both at the ribosome and in the cytosol: it binds, as a monomer, next to the exit channel at the ribosome to prevent the aggregation and premature folding of nascent polypeptides, while it functions as a dimer in the cytosol where is thought to assist in various processes in protein folding and biogenesis.
source: (iv) TF functions both at the ribosome and in the cytosol: it binds, as a monomer, next to the exit channel at the ribosome to prevent the aggregation and premature folding of nascent polypeptides, while it functions as a dimer in the cytosol where is thought to assist in various processes in protein folding and biogenesis (Agashe et al., 2004; Ferbitz et al., 2004; Haldar et al., 2017; Martinez-Hackert and Hendrickson, 2009; Oh et al., 2011; Ullers et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated with multiple supporting citations describing TF function.

claim: TF is being widely used as a co-expression factor to improve the folding and yield of soluble proteins in biotechnology.
source: TF is also being widely used as a co-expression factor to improve the folding and yield of soluble proteins in biotechnology (Uthailak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated with a citation describing biotechnology applications.

claim: Substrate protein binding causes TF to monomerize, thus indicating that the substrate-binding sites are occluded in dimeric TF.
source: Interestingly, our data showed that substrate protein binding causes TF to monomerize, thus indicating that the substrate-binding sites are occluded in dimeric TF.
evidence: This is an inference from experimental data showing monomerization upon substrate binding.

claim: The interplay between substrate protein binding and chaperone oligomerization is likely to be used as a mechanism to modulate the energetics and kinetics of interaction in chaperone-substrate protein complexes, as for example in small heat shock proteins.
source: The interplay between substrate protein binding and chaperone oligomerization is likely to be used as a mechanism to modulate the energetics and kinetics of interaction in chaperone-substrate protein complexes, as for example in small heat shock proteins (Eyles and Gierasch, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanism with a citation to similar behavior in other chaperones.

claim: The structure shows that three out of the five substrate-binding sites are partially buried in the dimer, thus explaining why protein binding results in TF monomerization.
source: The structure shows that three out of the five substrate-binding sites are partially buried in the dimer, thus explaining why protein binding results in TF monomerization.
evidence: This is a structural observation that explains the functional data on monomerization.

claim: The dimer assembles in such a way that substrate-binding sites in the two subunits form a large contiguous surface inside a cavity.
source: Interestingly, the dimer assembles in such a way that substrate-binding sites in the two subunits form a large contiguous surface inside a cavity.
evidence: This is a structural observation from the dimeric TF structure.

claim: The structural data explain the unexpected finding that non-native proteins appear to bind with higher association rate to the dimeric TF than to the monomeric TF.
source: The structural data explain the unexpected finding that non-native proteins appear to bind with higher association rate to the dimeric TF than to the monomeric TF.
evidence: This connects the structural observations with the kinetic measurements.

claim: Activity assays showed that TF dimerization enables the chaperone to exhibit stronger holdase and anti-aggregation activity.
source: Activity assays showed that TF dimerization enables the chaperone to exhibit stronger holdase and anti-aggregation activity.
evidence: This is a summary of the functional assay results presented.

claim: The RBD loop, which contains the signature motif (G43FRxGxxP50) mediating the interaction of TF with the ribosome, is sequestered by the PPD of the other subunit in the TF dimer and thus is not available for binding to the ribosome.
source: The RBD loop, which contains the signature motif (G43FRxGxxP50) mediating the interaction of TF with the ribosome, is sequestered by the PPD of the other subunit in the TF dimer and thus is not available for binding to the ribosome.
evidence: This is a structural observation that explains functional consequences.

claim: This finding explains why TF must monomerize upon binding to the ribosome.
source: This finding explains why TF must monomerize upon binding to the ribosome (Ferbitz et al., 2004).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data explaining previous observations.

claim: The intrinsic affinity of TF for the ribosome is Kd ~0.5 μM.
source: The intrinsic affinity of TF for the ribosome (Kaiser et al., 2006; Maier et al., 2003) (Kd ~0.5 μM; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) is comparable to the dimerization Kd (~2 μM); therefore, there is a strong competition between TF dimerization and ribosome binding.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments and cited literature.

claim: The intrinsic affinity of TF for the ribosome is comparable to the dimerization Kd (~2 μM); therefore, there is a strong competition between TF dimerization and ribosome binding.
source: The intrinsic affinity of TF for the ribosome (Kaiser et al., 2006; Maier et al., 2003) (Kd ~0.5 μM; Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) is comparable to the dimerization Kd (~2 μM); therefore, there is a strong competition between TF dimerization and ribosome binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing the measured Kd values.

claim: The affinity of TF for ribosome-nascent-chain (RNC) complexes is substantially stronger (Kd <0.01 μM) than for vacant ribosomes.
source: Because the affinity of TF for ribosome-nascent-chain (RNC) complexes is substantially stronger (Kd <0.01 μM) (Bornemann et al., 2014; Rutkowska et al., 2008) than for vacant ribosomes, translating ribosomes will be invariably bound, and thus protected by TF.
evidence: This is based on cited literature measuring TF affinity for RNC complexes.

claim: Translating ribosomes will be invariably bound, and thus protected by TF.
source: Because the affinity of TF for ribosome-nascent-chain (RNC) complexes is substantially stronger (Kd <0.01 μM) (Bornemann et al., 2014; Rutkowska et al., 2008) than for vacant ribosomes, translating ribosomes will be invariably bound, and thus protected by TF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the high affinity of TF for RNC complexes.

claim: When bound to the ribosome, TF is in the monomeric form and exposes all substrate-binding sites to the nascent protein.
source: When bound to the ribosome (Figure 6, panel i), TF is in the monomeric form and exposes all substrate-binding sites to the nascent protein.
evidence: This is based on structural and functional data presented in the study.

claim: The co-localization with the nascent chain results in TF delaying folding and preventing aggregation as shown before.
source: The co-localization with the nascent chain results in TF delaying folding and preventing aggregation as shown before (Agashe et al., 2004; Hoffmann et al., 2012; O'Brien et al., 2012; Saio et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited previous studies of TF function at the ribosome.

claim: As the nascent chain grows, additional TF molecules are recruited.
source: As the nascent chain grows, additional TF molecules are recruited (Figure 6, panel ii) (Kaiser et al., 2006).
evidence: This is based on cited literature describing TF recruitment during translation.

claim: Because of the high concentration of free TF in the cytoplasm, it is likely that a TF molecule outcompetes and displaces the fraction of the nascent chain that is bound to the TF to form a TF dimer.
source: Because of the high concentration of free TF in the cytoplasm, it is likely that a TF molecule outcompetes and displaces the fraction of the nascent chain that is bound to the TF to form a TF dimer.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the high cellular TF concentration and dimerization properties.

claim: Most cytosolic proteins released from the ribosome spontaneously form their native structure.
source: Most cytosolic proteins released from the ribosome (Figure 6, panel iv) spontaneously form their native structure (Balchin et al., 2016) (Figure 6, panel v).
evidence: This is based on cited literature describing protein folding in the cytoplasm.

claim: In the absence of molecular chaperones, many proteins have a tendency to aggregate.
source: However, in the absence of molecular chaperones, many proteins have a tendency to aggregate (Figure 6, panel vi).
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein behavior without chaperones.

claim: TF has an anti-aggregation activity, with the dimeric form being more potent than the monomeric form.
source: TF has an anti-aggregation activity, with the dimeric form being more potent than the monomeric form (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the aggregation assay data presented.

claim: Higher concentrations of monomeric TF are needed to achieve the same anti-aggregation activity as the dimeric TF.
source: This hypothesis is consistent with the following findings: (i) higher concentrations of monomeric TF are needed to achieve the same anti-aggregation activity as the dimeric TF (Figure 4C);
evidence: This is demonstrated by concentration-dependent aggregation assay data.

claim: Aggregation of shorter substrates, which are expected to bind to a single TF molecule, are equally prevented by the monomeric and dimeric TF.
source: and (ii) aggregation of shorter substrates, which are expected to bind to a single TF molecule, are equally prevented by the monomeric and dimeric TF (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by aggregation assay data with OmpA substrate.

claim: Depending on the energetics and kinetics of interaction between TF and the non-native polypeptide in the cytoplasm, dimeric TF can also function as a potent holdase chaperone to delay the folding of proteins destined for export, such as periplasmic and outer membrane proteins.
source: Depending on the energetics and kinetics of interaction between TF and the non-native polypeptide in the cytoplasm, dimeric TF can also function as a potent holdase chaperone (Figure 4E) to delay the folding of proteins destined for export, such as periplasmic and outer membrane proteins (Oh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on the holdase activity data and cited literature on TF function with export proteins.

claim: The activity of a chaperone can be modulated and tailored to specialized needs in the cell simply by a change in the oligomeric state of the chaperone, without the need of ATP binding and hydrolysis cycles or the binding of co-factors.
source: Our findings demonstrate how the activity of a chaperone can be modulated and tailored to specialized needs in the cell simply by a change in the oligomeric state of the chaperone, without the need of ATP binding and hydrolysis cycles or the binding of co-factors.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the data presented in the study.

claim: The large size of the dimeric TF (100 kDa) and its apparent dynamic nature has hindered determination of its structure.
source: The large size of the dimeric TF (100 kDa) and its apparent dynamic nature has hindered determination of its structure.
evidence: This explains why the structure was not previously determined.

claim: We have taken advantage of recent advances in NMR spectroscopy and isotope labeling to determine the atomic structure of dimeric TF.
source: We have taken advantage of recent advances in NMR spectroscopy and isotope labeling (Huang and Kalodimos, 2017) to determine the atomic structure of dimeric TF.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: Molecular chaperones typically prevent the aggregation and assist with the folding of non-native proteins.
source: Molecular chaperones typically prevent the aggregation and assist with the folding of non-native proteins (Balchin et al., 2016; Bukau et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge about chaperone function with supporting citations.

claim: Chaperones are central to protein homeostasis in the cell and are essential for life.
source: Thus, chaperones are central to protein homeostasis in the cell and are essential for life (Hipp et al., 2014; Powers and Balch, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the importance of chaperones with supporting citations.

claim: Recent studies have highlighted molecular chaperones as inhibitors of amyloid formation.
source: Recent studies have also highlighted molecular chaperones as inhibitors of amyloid formation (Mainz et al., 2015; Taylor et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited recent literature on chaperone function.

claim: Despite major advances in the field, how chaperones engage and alter the folding properties of non-native proteins remain poorly understood.
source: Despite major advances in the field, how chaperones engage and alter the folding properties of non-native proteins remain poorly understood (He et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2016; Koldewey et al., 2016; Libich et al., 2015; Rosenzweig et al., 2017; Saio et al., 2014; Sekhar et al., 2016; Verba et al., 2016; Wälti et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field with supporting citations.

claim: Despite common features, the mechanisms of activity are distinct in different families of chaperones.
source: Despite common features, the mechanisms of activity are distinct in different families of chaperones (Mattoo and Goloubinoff, 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited literature comparing different chaperone families.

claim: Studies of ATP-dependent chaperones, such as the Hsp70 and GroEL systems, have shown how cycles of ATP binding, hydrolysis and nucleotide release can give rise to different conformational states that exhibit distinct affinities for the substrate protein.
source: Studies of ATP-dependent chaperones, such as the Hsp70 and GroEL systems, have shown how cycles of ATP binding, hydrolysis and nucleotide release can give rise to different conformational states that exhibit distinct affinities for the substrate protein (Apetri and Horwich, 2008; Clare et al., 2012; Hayer-Hartl et al., 2016; Kampinga and Craig, 2010; Mayer and Bukau, 2005; Saibil et al., 2013; Sekhar et al., 2016; Zhuravleva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on extensive cited literature on ATP-dependent chaperones.

claim: Much less is known about how ATP-independent chaperones assist with protein folding.
source: Much less is known about how ATP-independent chaperones assist with protein folding (Stull et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: We used NMR spectroscopy to determine the atomic resolution structure of the 100 kDa dimeric TF.
source: We used NMR spectroscopy to determine the atomic resolution structure of the 100 kDa dimeric TF.
evidence: This describes the main methodological achievement of the study.

claim: Some of the substrate-binding sites are buried in the dimeric interface, explaining the lower affinity for protein substrates of the dimeric compared to the monomeric TF.
source: The structural data show that some of the substrate-binding sites are buried in the dimeric interface, explaining the lower affinity for protein substrates of the dimeric compared to the monomeric TF.
evidence: This is a structural observation that explains the measured affinity differences.

claim: The dimeric TF associates faster with proteins and it exhibits stronger anti-aggregation and holdase activity than the monomeric TF.
source: Surprisingly, the dimeric TF associates faster with proteins and it exhibits stronger anti-aggregation and holdase activity than the monomeric TF.
evidence: This is demonstrated by kinetic and functional assay data.

claim: The structural data show that the dimer assembles in a way that substrate-binding sites in the two subunits form a large contiguous surface inside a cavity, thus accounting for the observed accelerated association with unfolded proteins.
source: The structural data show that the dimer assembles in a way that substrate-binding sites in the two subunits form a large contiguous surface inside a cavity, thus accounting for the observed accelerated association with unfolded proteins.
evidence: This is a structural observation that explains the kinetic data.

claim: A hydrophobic patch in SBD arm 1 consisting of bulky hydrophobic residues (Leu314, Phe322, Leu332, Leu336, and Phe337) forms intimate nonpolar contacts with the C-terminal region of RBD helix α1 (Val35, Ala36, Val39, and Ile41).
source: Specifically, a hydrophobic patch in SBD arm 1 consisting of bulky hydrophobic residues (Leu314, Phe322, Leu332, Leu336, and Phe337) forms intimate nonpolar contacts with the C-terminal region of RBD helix α1 (Val35, Ala36, Val39, and Ile41) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the NMR structure.

claim: This binding interface is further strengthened by a salt bridge between Arg40 and Glu339 and a hydrogen bond between Lys38 and Gln340.
source: This binding interface is further strengthened by a salt bridge between Arg40 and Glu339 and a hydrogen bond between Lys38 and Gln340.
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the NMR structure.

claim: 2,540 Å2 (1,620 Å2 nonpolar and 920 Å2 polar) of surface are buried in the interface between SBD arm 1 and RBD of the dimer.
source: 2,540 Å2 (1,620 Å2 nonpolar and 920 Å2 polar) of surface are buried in this interface of the dimer.
evidence: This is a calculated value from the structural data.

claim: A large hydrophobic patch in PPD consisting of aromatic and bulky nonpolar residues (Phe168, Phe185, Met194, Ile195, Tyr221) engages the long loop in RBD connecting helices α1 and α3.
source: A large hydrophobic patch in PPD consisting of aromatic and bulky nonpolar residues (Phe168, Phe185, Met194, Ile195, Tyr221) engages the long loop in RBD connecting helices α1 and α3, which also features a short helix (α2).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the NMR structure.

claim: Residues Phe44, Val49, Ile53, and Tyr58 in RBD appear to establish the most important contacts with PPD, including two salt bridges (between Arg57 and Asp184 and between Lys48 and Glu199).
source: Residues Phe44, Val49, Ile53, and Tyr58 in RBD appear to establish the most important contacts with PPD, including two salt bridges (between Arg57 and Asp184 and between Lys48 and Glu199) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a detailed structural observation from the NMR structure.
